_help: Metro local flavor for the gamer on each box score page. Same knobs as data/flavor.json (see FLAVOR_HELP in mac/gamer.py). Notes are fact-checked against the source URL each carries.

lines.text: Canisius reached the NCAA tournament's regional finals in both 1955 and 1956.
In the 1956 NCAA tournament, Canisius beat No. 2 North Carolina State 79-78 in four overtimes at Madison Square Garden.
The Sporting News once ranked Canisius' 1956 NCAA tournament win over No. 2 North Carolina State, won on a Fran Corcoran shot, as the sixth-best upset in tournament history.
Joe Curran, who coached Canisius from 1953 to 1959, led the Griffins to three straight NCAA tournament appearances from 1955 to 1957.
Canisius has made four NCAA tournament appearances, the most recent in 1996, when the 13th-seeded Griffins met No. 4 Utah in Dallas.
Canisius won its first MAAC tournament title in 1996, beating Fairfield 52-46 in the final at Albany's Knickerbocker Arena.
Canisius reached the 1963 NIT final with wins over Memphis and Villanova before losing to Providence.
Canisius reached the 1995 NIT semifinals with wins over Seton Hall, Bradley and Washington State.
Canisius went 15-3 in MAAC play in 2017-18 to share the league's regular-season title with Rider.
Ray Hall is the Canisius career scoring leader with 2,226 points from 1981-82 through 1984-85.
Hank Nowak holds the Canisius career rebounding record with 880 from 1954-55 through 1956-57.
The Canisius single-game rebounding record belongs to Larry Fogle, who grabbed 26 against Catholic in 1973-74.
Canisius was founded in Buffalo in 1870 by German Jesuits, is named for St. Peter Canisius and officially became Canisius University on Aug. 1, 2023.
Science Hall on the Canisius campus in Buffalo was built in 1929 as a Sears and Roebuck store.
Canisius is the only NCAA Division I school that uses Griffins as its mascot name.
The Canisius griffin mascot was named Petey in a 2002 student vote, and the school's first costumed griffin appeared on the sidelines in 1967-68.
In his history of Canisius, Charles A. Brady traced the school's Griffin to La Salle's ship the Griffon, which he called the first ship built on America's inland seas.
Canisius alum Mike Smrek, a 1985 second-round pick of the Portland Trail Blazers, won NBA titles with the Los Angeles Lakers in 1987 and 1988.
Canisius All-American Johnny McCarthy won an NBA title with the 1964 Boston Celtics and had a triple-double in his 1960 playoff debut with the St. Louis Hawks.
John Beilein went 89-62 in five seasons at Canisius from 1992 to 1997 before later coaching Michigan to two national title games.
Michael Meeks, MVP of the 1996 MAAC tournament for Canisius, later led Canada in scoring at the 2000 Olympics.
Teressa Bellissimo is credited with inventing the Buffalo wing in 1964 at the Anchor Bar, which stands at 1047 Main Street, the same street as the Canisius campus.
Niagara Falls lies about 20 miles northwest of downtown Buffalo, home of Canisius.
Buffalo sits where Lake Erie narrows into the Niagara River, and its Peace Bridge has linked the city to Fort Erie, Ontario, since 1927.
The Erie Canal reached its western end on the Buffalo waterfront in 1825, an area now known as Canalside.
Buffalo, New York's second-largest city, is home to more than a half-dozen Frank Lloyd Wright designs, including the Martin House.
Beyond wings, Buffalo's regional specialties include beef on weck, sponge candy and the chicken finger sub.
Frederick Law Olmsted began planning Buffalo's park system in 1868, and it now includes six parks linked by seven parkways.
Canisius and Niagara play the Battle of the Bridge, named for the Grand Island Bridge that both teams cross to reach the other's campus 24 miles away.
Canisius and Niagara first met in basketball on Dec. 1, 1904, when Canisius won 2-0.
Canisius and Niagara created the all-sports Canal Cup in 2007, named for the Erie Canal that separates Erie County from Niagara County.
Canisius, Niagara and St. Bonaventure made up the Little Three, whose rivalry filled Buffalo's Memorial Auditorium on Saturday nights.
Jim Christian was hired on April 8, 2024, as the 25th head coach in Canisius history after head jobs at Kent State, TCU, Ohio and Boston College.
Canisius coach Jim Christian went 138-58 at Kent State from 2002 to 2008 and took the Golden Flashes to the NCAA tournament in 2006 and 2008.
Canisius went 10-21 and 5-15 in the MAAC in 2025-26, Jim Christian's second season, up from 3-28 the year before.
Canisius opened the 2026-27 season on Nov. 2 at Penn State, the earliest start date in program history.
Canisius plays in the Metro Conference, which took that name on July 1, 2026, after 45 years as the Metro Atlantic Athletic Conference.
Canisius opens Metro Conference play at home against Rider on Dec. 4.
Canisius visits Niagara on Jan. 24 for the 198th meeting between the schools and hosts the Purple Eagles on Feb. 11.
Canisius visits Syracuse on Dec. 16 for the 72nd meeting between the two schools.

home_lines.text: The Koessler Athletic Center on the Canisius campus was built in 1968 at a cost of $3 million and seats 2,196 for basketball.
The Koessler Athletic Center is named for J. Walter Koessler, a member of the Canisius class of 1922.
A $1.3 million renovation completed in 2002 removed the ceiling of the Koessler Athletic Center gym and replaced its bleachers with 1,100 chair-back seats and new bleachers.

lines.text: Iona holds the league record with 14 conference tournament championships, won in 1982, 1984, 1985, 1998, 2000, 2001, 2006, 2013, 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019, 2021 and 2023.
Iona has made 16 NCAA Tournament appearances, the first in 1979 and the most recent in 2023.
Iona won four straight MAAC tournament titles from 2016 through 2019, a league first, finishing the run with an 81-60 win over Monmouth in Albany.
Rickey McGill left Iona in 2019 as the only player in MAAC history with four championship rings, having gone 12-0 in the league tournament.
On Feb. 21, 1980, Iona beat No. 2 Louisville 77-60 at Madison Square Garden, the last loss for a Louisville team that went on to win the national title.
Iona beat No. 22 North Carolina 65-56 at Madison Square Garden on Dec. 27, 2002, and beat No. 10 Alabama 72-68 in Orlando on Nov. 25, 2021.
Iona has won 13 regular-season league titles, starting with three straight from 1983 to 1985 and most recently in 2022 and 2023.
Iona was a charter member in 1980 of the league now called the Metro Conference, along with Army, Fairfield, Fordham, Manhattan and Saint Peter's.
Steve Burtt of the Class of 1984 holds Iona's career scoring record with 2,534 points, and Steve Burtt of the Class of 2006 ranks second with 2,034.
Warren Isaac holds Iona's single-game scoring mark with 50 points against Bates on Dec. 18, 1964.
The first jersey number Iona ever retired was Richie Guerin's No. 14, unveiled at halftime of a game against Manhattan at the Hynes Center on Jan. 31, 2014.
New Rochelle, home of Iona, was settled in 1688 by 33 Huguenot families, and the settlers named it for La Rochelle, France.
New Rochelle, home of Iona, carries the nickname Queen City of the Sound, taken from a 1926 poem of the same name by James J. Montague.
New Rochelle, home of Iona, is about 17 miles from Midtown Manhattan.
New Rochelle, home of Iona, is the site of the Thomas Paine Cottage, built in 1793 and now a National Historic Landmark.
On The Dick Van Dyke Show, the Petrie family lived in New Rochelle, home of Iona, at 148 Bonnie Meadow Road.
New Rochelle's Glen Island covers about 105 acres, has a crescent-shaped beach on Long Island Sound and is linked to the mainland by a drawbridge built in the 1920s.
Iona was founded in 1940 by the Christian Brothers in New Rochelle and became Iona University on July 1, 2022.
Iona takes its name from the Iona School in New Rochelle, which its first principal, Br. Joseph Ignatius Doorley, named for St. Columba's island monastery in 1916.
Iona's men's basketball team was christened the Gaels when it began play in 1940, a nod to Irish heritage, and the school's costumed mascot is Killian.
Richie Guerin, Iona Class of 1954, scored 1,375 points for the Gaels and went on to six NBA All-Star selections and the Naismith Hall of Fame.
Jeff Ruland led Iona to a 69-21 record over three seasons and its first two NCAA Tournament appearances before Golden State drafted him 25th overall in 1981.
Walter Clayton Jr. was the 2023 MAAC Player of the Year at Iona and later the 2025 Final Four Most Outstanding Player for national champion Florida.
Iona point guard Scott Machado led the nation with 9.9 assists per game in 2011-12 and signed with the Houston Rockets in September 2012.
Jim Valvano went 95-46 as Iona coach from 1975 to 1980 and also served as the school's athletic director from 1977 to 1980.
Under Tim Cluess, Iona reached the NCAA Tournament six times in nine seasons and won five MAAC tournament titles.
Rick Pitino went 64-22 in three seasons at Iona, reaching two NCAA Tournaments and winning the regular-season league title in 2022 and 2023.
Iona coach Dan Geriot, a former Richmond player, was hired on March 20, 2025, after nine years as a Cleveland Cavaliers assistant and one with the New Orleans Pelicans.
Dan Geriot's first Iona team went 18-14 overall and 10-10 in the league in 2025-26.
Iona opened the 2026-27 season with a 56-55 home win over Vermont on Nov. 2, 2026, as Kevon Vanderhorst scored 27 points.
Iona is playing its first season in the Metro Conference, the name the former MAAC took on July 1, 2026, partly to end confusion with the Mid-American Conference.
The 2027 Metro Conference tournament, which includes Iona, runs March 4-9 at Boardwalk Hall in Atlantic City, the eighth straight season the event has been held there.
Iona and Manhattan, two charter members of the league, have played men's basketball against each other since 1946.
Iona closed the 2025-26 regular season with a 69-65 win over Manhattan at Draddy Gymnasium in Riverdale on March 1, 2026.
Iona and Fairfield have met more than 125 times in men's basketball, and Iona led the series 78-48 entering their January 2026 meeting.

home_lines.text: A banner honoring former Iona coach Jim Valvano has hung in the Hynes Center since Jan. 7, 2024, making him the second Gael honored with a banner there after Richie Guerin.
The Hynes Athletics Center opened on Iona's New Rochelle campus in 1974 and seats 2,578 for basketball.
The Hynes Center is named for James P. Hynes, Iona Class of 1969 and a former chairman of the board of trustees, and his wife, Anne Marie Hynes.
Before it took the Hynes name in 2005, Iona's gym was known as the John A. Mulcahy Campus Events Center for its first 31 years.
A 2019 renovation of Iona's Hynes Center, backed by a lead gift from Edward F. Arrigoni, put retractable seating on all four sides of the court and added LED scoreboards and ribbon boards.
Fans entering Iona's Hynes Center at 715 North Avenue pass the Arrigoni Hall of Excellence, which displays the school's championship trophies and memorabilia.
Iona's Hynes Center was also home in 1986 to the Westchester Golden Apples of the United States Basketball League.

lines.text: Manhattan University was founded in 1853 as the Academy of the Holy Infancy by five French De La Salle Christian Brothers.
Manhattan began in a small building on Canal Street and later moved to 131st Street and Broadway in Manhattanville before settling in the Riverdale section of the Bronx in 1922.
Manhattan received its state charter as Manhattan College in 1863 and was renamed Manhattan University in 2024.
The Baseball Hall of Fame credits Manhattan with the seventh-inning stretch, traced to Brother Jasper calling time-out and telling students to stand up and stretch.
Manhattan's colors are kelly green and white, and its men's teams are called the Jaspers.
Manhattan's North campus overlooks Van Cortlandt Park, which the school uses for outdoor track and field, golf and cross country.
Manhattan's Riverdale campus is near the Van Cortlandt Park-242nd Street station on the 1 train, with Metro-North's Riverdale station on the Hudson Line farther west.
Manhattan University Pipes and Drums, established in 1981, marches in the New York City Saint Patrick's Day Parade.
Manhattan's student newspaper, The Quadrangle, has published continually since 1924 and comes out weekly on Tuesdays during the academic year.
Manhattan's alumni include Edgar Award-winning novelist James Patterson.
Fairfield first fielded a men's basketball team in 1948-49, going 9-14 under coach Joe Dunn.
Fairfield has reached the NCAA Division I tournament three times, in 1986, 1987 and 1997, each time after winning its conference tournament.
In the 1997 NCAA tournament, Fairfield led top-seeded North Carolina by seven points at halftime before falling 82-74.
Fairfield won back-to-back conference tournament titles in 1986 and 1987 under coach Mitch Buonaguro.
Fairfield beat Marshall 80-76 in the 1973 NIT and Colorado State 62-60 in the 2011 NIT.
Fairfield erased a 27-point deficit to beat George Mason 101-96 in overtime in the 2010 CIT, the largest comeback in Division I postseason history.
Fairfield made three straight NCAA Division II tournaments from 1960 to 1962 under coach George Bisacca.
Fairfield is one of six charter members of the league founded in 1980 as the Metro Atlantic Athletic Conference, which became the Metro Conference on July 1, 2026.
Fairfield won MAAC regular-season championships in 1986 and 2011.
Fairfield reached the semifinals of the College Basketball Invitational in 2024, winning two games before a 75-58 loss to Seattle.
Fred Barakat's 160 wins from 1970 to 1981 are the most by a Fairfield men's basketball coach, and he took the Stags to the NIT in 1973, 1974 and 1978.
Darren Phillip of Fairfield led the nation in rebounding in 2001, and Deng Gai of Fairfield led it in blocked shots in 2005.
The town of Fairfield was founded in 1639 by Roger Ludlowe, who bought land then known as Unquowa.
Fairfield has about five miles of coastline on Long Island Sound and five town beaches staffed by lifeguards in summer.
General Electric kept its corporate headquarters in Fairfield for more than four decades before moving to Boston in 2017.
Bigelow Tea is headquartered on Black Rock Turnpike in Fairfield.
Fairfield University's campus sits less than 60 miles from New York City, about an hour and 20 minutes by Metro-North Railroad.
Fairfield counted 61,512 residents in the 2020 census and is home to two universities, Fairfield and Sacred Heart, which together enroll more than 17,000 students.
Fairfield's teams were known as the Men in Red in 1947-48 before a board vote chose Stags over Chanticleers.
The Stags name nods to Fairfield's place in the Diocese of Hartford, since a hart is a male deer, and the university seal shows a deer leaping a brook.
Fairfield's student section, Stags in the Stands, was founded in 2005, following the Red Sea fan base that filled Alumni Hall in the 1970s.
Fairfield's mascot is Lucas the Stag, and the school colors are red and white.

Fairfield University was founded in 1942 when the Jesuits acquired two adjoining estates, and its 200-acre campus still includes Bellarmine Hall, built in 1921 as the Lashar family's Hearthstone Hall.
Thirteen Fairfield players have been drafted or signed by NBA teams, among them A.J. Wynder with the Boston Celtics and Deng Gai with the Philadelphia 76ers.
Fairfield had two players selected in the 1979 NBA draft, Joe DeSantis and Mark Young.
Ed Cooley went 92-69 as Fairfield's coach from 2006 to 2011 and was named the Ben Jobe National Coach of the Year in 2010.
Chris Casey's first Fairfield team went 22-12 in 2023-24 and reached the conference tournament title game.
Fairfield went 21-13 last season and 11-9 in league play, then won two conference tournament games as the No. 7 seed before losing to Siena.
Fairfield and Sacred Heart are both located in Fairfield, and they became conference opponents when Sacred Heart joined the league for the 2024-25 season.
Fairfield won 92-87 at crosstown Sacred Heart last season, a year after Sacred Heart beat the Stags in the first round of the 2025 conference tournament.
Fairfield won 85-79 on the road last season at Quinnipiac, its in-state conference rival from Hamden.
Fairfield, Iona, Manhattan and Saint Peter's are the four charter members from 1980 still playing in the Metro Conference.

home_lines.text: Leo D. Mahoney Arena, Fairfield's 3,500-seat home on Loyola Drive, opened on Nov. 18, 2022, on the site of the old Alumni Hall.
Fairfield's Mahoney Arena cost $51 million and was fully funded by donors.
The court at Fairfield's Mahoney Arena is named for George Bisacca, the former coach and athletic director, a name carried over from Alumni Hall.
Mahoney Arena is named for Leo D. Mahoney, a former Fairfield University trustee whose family's gift was the largest in school history.
Deon Perry's 70-foot shot at the buzzer beat Marist at Fairfield's Mahoney Arena on Feb. 6, 2025, in a game televised nationally on ESPNU.

lines.text: Marist first fielded a men's basketball team in 1961-62 as a Division III program and moved up to Division I ahead of the 1981-82 season.
Marist's two NCAA tournament trips came in back-to-back years, a 68-53 first-round loss to Georgia Tech in 1986 and a 93-68 first-round loss to Pittsburgh in 1987.
Marist won the ECAC Metro Conference tournament in 1986 and 1987.
The 1987 Marist team went 15-1 in conference play on its way to the program's second straight NCAA tournament bid.
Marist finished first in the MAAC in 2006-07, then beat Oklahoma State 67-64 in the NIT before falling to NC State 69-66 in the second round.
Marist lost 82-77 to Rhode Island in the first round of the 1996 NIT.
Before its Division I days, Marist reached the 1973 NAIA tournament and lost 81-65 to Xavier of Louisiana in the first round.
Marist has retired three men's basketball numbers: Drafton Davis' No. 3, Steve Smith's No. 12 and Rik Smits' No. 45.
Marist was a charter member of the ECAC Metro Conference in 1981 and joined the MAAC in 1997.
Dave Magarity coached Marist for 18 seasons, from 1986 to 2004, and won 253 games with the Red Foxes.
Ron Petro coached Marist from 1966 to 1984, winning 226 games and guiding the Red Foxes through their move to Division I.
Rik Smits was the No. 2 pick of the 1988 NBA draft and became the first Marist player to play in the NBA.
Jared Jordan became the second Marist player drafted by the NBA when the Los Angeles Clippers took him 45th overall in 2007.
Poughkeepsie sits about 75 miles north of Manhattan and is the northern terminus of Metro-North's Hudson Line.
Poughkeepsie, chartered as a city in 1854, is known as the Queen City of the Hudson.
Poughkeepsie became the second capital of the State of New York after Kingston was burned by the British.
Poughkeepsie remains IBM's primary design and manufacturing center for its newest mainframes, on a site that once built the IBM 7030 Stretch.
Smith Brothers cough drops were made in a Poughkeepsie factory until 1972.
Poughkeepsie takes its name from a Munsee word meaning the reed-covered lodge by the little-water place, a reference to a spring or stream feeding the Hudson River.
Poughkeepsie's Hudson River crossings include the Mid-Hudson Bridge, opened in 1930, and the Walkway Over the Hudson, opened on Oct. 3, 2009.
Marist's 180-acre campus runs along U.S. Route 9 on the east bank of the Hudson River in the town of Poughkeepsie.
Marist shares Poughkeepsie with Vassar College, founded by Matthew Vassar in 1861.
Marist's red and white colors come from the red fox, an animal native to the Hudson Valley.
Marist's fox mascot has answered to Frankie since 2017, when the school dropped the name Shooter.
The school in Poughkeepsie has been called Marist Normal Training School, Marian College and Marist College, and it became Marist University on Jan. 29, 2025.
Marist traces its roots to 1905, when the Marist Brothers arrived in the Mid-Hudson Valley and named their property Saint Ann's Hermitage.
Marist's rowers compete against Army each spring for the President's Cup Trophy.
Greystone, St. Peter's and the Kieran Gatehouse on Marist's campus are 1860s-era buildings listed on the National Register of Historic Places.
John Dunne, a Queens native who played at Ithaca College from 1988 to 1992, has coached Marist since April 3, 2018.
Before coming to Marist, John Dunne won the 2011 MAAC tournament and the 2017 CIT championship as head coach at Saint Peter's.
John Dunne is in his ninth season at Marist and came into 2026-27 with a 115-122 record in Poughkeepsie.
Marist finished 19-12 last season and 12-8 in league play, and its year ended with a 58-57 loss to top-seeded Merrimack in the conference semifinals.
Marist was the No. 5 seed in last season's conference tournament and beat fourth-seeded Quinnipiac 77-75 in the quarterfinals.
Marist won 57 games over the previous three seasons under John Dunne, going 18-13, 20-10 and 19-12.
Marist's fiercest rivalry is with Siena, a men's basketball series often called the Battle of I-87.
Marist coach John Dunne knows the other side of the Battle of I-87, having worked as an assistant at Siena from 1999 to 2001.
John Dunne went 153-225 in 12 seasons as head coach at Saint Peter's before Marist hired him in 2018.

home_lines.text: McCann Arena, built in 1977, seats 3,200 for Marist basketball in Poughkeepsie.
McCann Arena carries the name of James J. McCann, born in Poughkeepsie in 1880, whose family ran the McCann Feed and Grain Store and who set up the McCann Foundation in 1967.
The maple floor at McCann Arena was a gift from Rik Smits, and when a fire sprinkler soaked that court, the former Marist center donated another.
A display honoring Rik Smits, complete with an Indiana Pacers jersey, sits beside the court at Marist's McCann Arena.
The student section at Marist's McCann Arena rises 19 feet along the south baseline, with seats less than 6 feet from the baseline.
A 2011 renovation gave Marist's McCann Arena chair-back seats in place of bleachers, new corner seating and video scoreboards in two corners.
Press row at Marist's McCann Arena is a 40-foot NBA-style scorer's table installed in a 2005 renovation.

lines.text: Merrimack played its first men's basketball season in 1949 and went 7-2 under Paul Lanni, its first head coach.
Merrimack won the Northeast Conference regular-season title outright in 2019-20, its first Division I season, going 20-11 overall and 14-4 in the league.
Merrimack in 2019-20 became the first men's basketball team to record a 20-win season in its first Division I season.
Merrimack beat Fairleigh Dickinson 67-66 in the 2023 Northeast Conference final in North Andover and finished that season on an 11-game winning streak.
Merrimack won Northeast Conference regular-season titles in 2020, 2023 and 2024.
Merrimack won Northeast-10 tournament titles in 1992, 2000 and 2019 during its run in that Division II league from 1984 to 2019.
Merrimack's single-game scoring record is the 52 points Steve McMahon scored in 1971-72, and in 1972 he became the first Warrior drafted into the NBA.
Ed Murphy, Merrimack's career scoring leader with 2,874 points, averaged 32.0 points in 1976-77 and was drafted by the Atlanta Hawks in 1978.
Roger Damphousse became the first Merrimack basketball player named an All-American in 1961.
Merrimack began a four-year move from Division II in 2019-20 and became a full Division I member in 2023-24.
North Andover, home of Merrimack College, was the north parish of Andover until it was incorporated as its own town on April 7, 1855.
Merrimack's 220-acre campus in North Andover sits 25 miles north of downtown Boston.
North Andover, where Merrimack plays, was the headquarters of sneaker maker Converse from 2002 to 2015.
Merrimack's hometown of North Andover is home to Barker's Farm, started in 1643 and the oldest continually operated business in Massachusetts.
Lake Cochichewick dominates the northeastern quadrant of North Andover, the Essex County town of 30,915 at the 2020 census where Merrimack College sits.
North Andover, Merrimack's hometown, holds a sheep shearing festival in its old town center in late spring.
Merrimack College was founded in 1947 by the Order of Saint Augustine to educate World War II veterans and opened that September.
Merrimack's colors are navy blue and gold, and its mascot is Mack the Warrior.
Merrimack counts baseball player Carl Yastrzemski and actor Charlie Day among its alumni.
Former Merrimack player Jordan Minor signed with the Long Island Nets in 2024.
Juvaris Hayes became the first Merrimack player named a Division I All-American.
Merrimack coach Joe Gallo played guard for the Warriors from 2000 to 2004 and began his coaching career as a Merrimack assistant in 2005 before returning as head coach in 2016.
Merrimack coach Joe Gallo, a native of Milltown, New Jersey, was an assistant at Dartmouth and Robert Morris before returning to his alma mater.
Joe Gallo took Merrimack to the NCAA Division II tournament in each of his first three seasons as head coach.
Merrimack coach Joe Gallo was named MAAC Coach of the Year in 2026.
Merrimack went 23-11 last season, a program record for wins, and took its first MAAC regular-season title at 17-3.
Merrimack has never appeared in the Division I NCAA tournament.
Merrimack beat Sacred Heart 70-48 in the 2026 MAAC quarterfinals at Boardwalk Hall in Atlantic City.
Siena beat Merrimack 64-54 in the 2026 MAAC final at Boardwalk Hall after the Warriors had won both regular-season meetings.

home_lines.text: Merrimack's Lawler Arena is named for J. Thom Lawler, the former Warriors hockey coach who led the team to its first national title in 1978.
Merrimack's Lawler Arena seats 2,549 for hockey, and its basketball setup raises capacity to 3,000.
Merrimack's athletics complex in North Andover opened on Nov. 28, 1972.
Merrimack went 11-0 at Lawler Arena in 2025-26, its first unbeaten home record since 1990-91.

lines.text: Mount St. Mary's won the NCAA College Division national championship in 1962, the only national title in program history.
Mount St. Mary's finished as the NCAA Division II runner-up in 1981, 19 years after winning the College Division title.
Mount St. Mary's made 14 NCAA Division II and College Division tournament appearances, going 25-17 and reaching the Final Four in 1957, 1961, 1962, 1981 and 1985.
Mount St. Mary's has made seven NCAA Division I tournament appearances, in 1995, 1999, 2008, 2014, 2017, 2021 and 2025, and owns a 3-7 record in them.
Mount St. Mary's first NCAA Division I tournament game came in 1995, a 113-67 loss to top-seeded Kentucky.
Mount St. Mary's drew top-seeded Michigan State in the 1999 NCAA tournament and lost 76-53.
Mount St. Mary's earned its first NCAA Division I tournament win in 2008, beating Coppin State 69-60 before a 113-74 loss to top-seeded North Carolina.
Mount St. Mary's beat New Orleans by a single point, 67-66, in the 2017 NCAA tournament before falling 76-56 to top-seeded Villanova.
Mount St. Mary's most recent NCAA tournament win came in 2025, an 83-72 decision over American that was followed by a 93-49 loss to top-seeded Duke.
All three of Mount St. Mary's NCAA Division I tournament wins have come against fellow 16 seeds: Coppin State in 2008, New Orleans in 2017 and American in 2025.
Mount St. Mary's NCAA tournament trips in 2014 and 2021 both ended in the First Four, with a 71-64 loss to Albany and a 60-52 loss to Texas Southern.
Mount St. Mary's won six Northeast Conference tournament titles, in 1995, 1999, 2008, 2014, 2017 and 2021, as a member of that league from 1989 to 2022.
Mount St. Mary's won Northeast Conference regular-season titles in 1996 and 2017.
Mount St. Mary's played in the Northeast Conference from 1989 to 2022 before joining the MAAC on July 1, 2022.
Mount St. Mary's won its first MAAC tournament title in 2025 after joining the league on July 1, 2022.
Mount St. Mary's won 11 Mason-Dixon Conference tournament titles, the first in 1944 and the last in 1988.
Mount St. Mary's lone NIT appearance came in 1996, a 73-49 first-round loss to Illinois State.
Mount St. Mary's played in the CollegeInsider.com Tournament once, losing 69-58 to James Madison in the first round in 2009.
Jim Phelan coached Mount St. Mary's for 49 years, won 830 of his 1,354 games and was inducted into the National Collegiate Basketball Hall of Fame in 2008.
Donny Lind has been the head coach at Mount St. Mary's since April 20, 2024.

home_lines.text: Knott Arena, the home of Mount St. Mary's basketball in Emmitsburg, opened in 1987.
The court at Knott Arena in Emmitsburg has carried the name of Jim Phelan, who won a school-record 830 games at Mount St. Mary's between 1954 and 2003, since 2006.
Knott Arena, where Mount St. Mary's plays in Emmitsburg, has also hosted high school graduation ceremonies for Frederick County Public Schools.
The concourse at Mount St. Mary's Knott Arena was remodeled in 2024 and dedicated to former athletic director Lynne Phelan Robinson.

lines.text: Niagara has played in three NCAA Tournaments, in 1970, 2005 and 2007, and holds a 2-4 record in the event.
Niagara's first NCAA Tournament win came in 1970, a 79-69 first-round decision over Pennsylvania.
Niagara's most recent NCAA Tournament victory was a 77-69 win over Florida A&M in the 2007 opening round.
Niagara has made 14 trips to the NIT, finishing third in 1954 and reaching the championship game against Maryland in 1972.
Niagara won MAAC regular-season titles in 1999, 2005 and 2013 and took the conference tournament in 2005 and 2007.
Niagara's 2008-09 team holds the program record for wins, finishing 26-9.
Niagara's coaching records begin in 1905-06, when Charles McGrath's team went 4-2.
Niagara has retired the numbers of nine players, among them Calvin Murphy's No. 23 and Larry Costello's No. 69.
John Blake coached Niagara from 1918 to 1923 and went 61-14, a .813 winning percentage.
Niagara was a member of the Western New York Little Three Conference from 1946 to 1958.
Niagara twice left campus for the Niagara Falls Convention and Civic Center, playing home games there from 1973 to 1982 and from 1988 to 1996.
Taps Gallagher's Niagara teams won 11 Little Three championships and made seven NIT appearances.
Frank Layden coached Niagara from 1968 to 1976 and led the Purple Eagles to their first NCAA Tournament in 1970 before a 23-year NBA coaching career.
Niagara University was founded on Nov. 21, 1856, as Our Lady of Angels Seminary by the Congregation of the Mission.
Niagara's campus in Lewiston is home to the Castellani Art Museum, which holds more than 5,700 works.
Niagara University opened a law school in Buffalo in 1887.
Niagara's colors are purple and white, and its mascot is Monte.
Niagara first played football in 1897 and dropped the sport for the final time after the 1987 season.
Basketball shares the winter at Niagara with a hockey team that plays at Dwyer Arena and has reached the NCAA Tournament four times, in 2000, 2004, 2008 and 2013.
Greg Paulus has led Niagara since October 2019, when he was promoted from assistant to interim head coach.
Greg Paulus' Niagara staff this season includes assistants Chris Buchanan, Will Holland, Jake Presutti and Charles Chigeru.

home_lines.text: The Gallagher Center opened on Niagara's campus in Lewiston on Nov. 30, 1949, and seats 2,400.
Niagara's home gym was known as the Niagara University Student Center until May 23, 1982, when it was renamed for longtime coach John J. Gallagher.
The Gallagher Center in Lewiston carries the name of Taps Gallagher, who coached Niagara for 31 seasons and had 25 winning ones.
The floor at Niagara's Gallagher Center has been called Layden Court since 2014, in honor of former coach Frank Layden and his wife, Barbara.

lines.text: Quinnipiac made NCAA Division II tournament appearances in 1976, 1979, 1980 and 1988.
Quinnipiac played in the NAIA tournament in 1972 and 1973, beating Ouachita Baptist in the second of those trips.
Quinnipiac won the Northeast Conference regular-season title in 2010 and went to the NIT that March, where it lost to Virginia Tech 81-61.
Quinnipiac won back-to-back MAAC regular-season championships in 2024 and 2025, going 15-5 in league play both years.
Quinnipiac went 24-10 in 2023-24 and finished its season in the CBI at Daytona Beach, Florida.
Quinnipiac and Monmouth joined the MAAC in July 2013, replacing Loyola University Maryland.
Joe DeSantis coached Quinnipiac for 11 years, led the move from Division II to Division I and was Northeast Conference coach of the year in 1999-2000, when the team went 18-10.
Quinnipiac's teams were the Braves until 2002, when the school in Hamden adopted the Bobcats nickname.
Quinnipiac's mascot is Boomer the Bobcat, its fight song is called The Bobcat Roar and its colors are navy and gold.
Quinnipiac was founded in 1929 in New Haven as the Connecticut College of Commerce and moved to the Mount Carmel section of Hamden in 1966.
Quinnipiac took its name in 1951 in honor of the Quinnipiac tribe, which once lived in what is now Greater New Haven.
Before moving up to York Hill, Quinnipiac played from 1969 at 2,000-seat Burt Kahn Court, where it went 254-184.
Burt Kahn Court, Quinnipiac's old basketball gym in Hamden, is named for a former Quinnipiac basketball coach and athletic director and is now home to the volleyball team.
Hamden, home of Quinnipiac, is nicknamed the Land of the Sleeping Giant.
Quinnipiac University sits at the foot of Sleeping Giant, a traprock mountain about eight miles north of New Haven with a high point of 739 feet.
The stone tower atop Sleeping Giant, the mountain above Quinnipiac's campus in Hamden, was built by the Works Progress Administration in 1936.
More than 30 miles of hiking trails cross Sleeping Giant, the mountain next door to Quinnipiac in Hamden, including five miles of the 23-mile Quinnipiac Trail.
Hamden, home of Quinnipiac, became a separate town in 1786, when about 1,400 residents incorporated it, and is named for the English statesman John Hampden.
Eli Whitney made arms for the U.S. government at a mill site in Hamden, Quinnipiac's hometown, where he introduced interchangeable parts.
The Farmington Canal carried boats through Hamden from 1825 to 1848, and its old right-of-way is now a walking and bicycling trail through Quinnipiac's hometown.
Hamden, where Quinnipiac plays, counted 61,169 residents in the 2020 census and borders New Haven to the south.
The first truss bridge in the United States was built over the Mill River in 1823 in the Whitneyville section of Hamden, the town Quinnipiac calls home.
Quinnipiac's alumni include Murray Lender, the former chief executive of Lender's Bagels.
Quinnipiac basketball alumni James Feldeine and Cameron Young have both played in the Israeli Basketball Premier League.
Tom Pecora, a native of Queens Village, New York, joined Quinnipiac as associate head coach in March 2017 and was promoted to head coach on April 13, 2023.
Before Quinnipiac, Tom Pecora won 155 games in nine seasons as head coach at Hofstra and then spent five seasons leading Fordham.
Tom Pecora was named MAAC coach of the year in each of his first two seasons leading Quinnipiac, 2024 and 2025.
Quinnipiac went 19-13 last season and 12-8 in the league, then lost 77-75 to Marist as the No. 4 seed in the conference quarterfinals at Boardwalk Hall.
This is Quinnipiac's first season in the Metro Conference, the name the MAAC took on July 1, 2026.
Quinnipiac is one of three Connecticut schools in the 13-team league, along with Fairfield and Sacred Heart, which are both in the town of Fairfield.
Quinnipiac gained a second in-state league opponent when Sacred Heart joined the conference for the 2024-25 season, the same year Merrimack arrived.
Former Quinnipiac coach Joe DeSantis earned All-American honors as a player at Fairfield in 1979.

home_lines.text: M&T Bank Arena opened on Quinnipiac's York Hill campus in Hamden on Jan. 27, 2007, at a cost of $52 million.
Quinnipiac's M&T Bank Arena seats 3,570 for basketball and 3,386 for hockey.
Quinnipiac's home at 305 Sherman Avenue in Hamden has carried four names since 2007: TD Banknorth Sports Center, TD Bank Sports Center, People's United Center and M&T Bank Arena.
The hockey arena inside Quinnipiac's M&T Bank Arena in Hamden is named the Frank Perrotti, Jr. Arena.
Ground was broken on Quinnipiac's York Hill arena in Hamden on Oct. 7, 2004.

lines.text: Sacred Heart played its first men's basketball season in 1965-66 under coach Don Feeley.
Sacred Heart won the 1986 NCAA Division II national championship with a 93-87 victory over Southeast Missouri State in Springfield, Massachusetts.
Sacred Heart's Roger Younger was named Most Outstanding Player of the 1986 NCAA Division II tournament, which the Pioneers won.
Sacred Heart made 13 NCAA Division II tournament appearances and went 22-15 in those games.
Sacred Heart reached the Division II Final Four in 1977 and 1986 and the Elite Eight seven times between 1977 and 1989.
Sacred Heart has played in Division I since 1999-2000 and has not yet appeared in the NCAA Division I tournament.
Sacred Heart played in the Northeast Conference from 1999-2000 through 2023-24 before moving to the league now known as the Metro Conference.
Sacred Heart's first conference win after leaving the Northeast Conference was an 83-59 home victory over Iona on Dec. 6, 2024.
Sacred Heart played its home games at Memorial Hall from 1965-66 through 1996-97 before moving into the William H. Pitt Center.
Fairfield, the Connecticut town Sacred Heart calls home, was founded in 1639 by Roger Ludlowe on land then called Unquowa.
Fairfield, home of Sacred Heart, has five miles of Long Island Sound coastline and five town beaches.
Sacred Heart's hometown of Fairfield counted 61,512 residents in 2020 and borders Bridgeport, Trumbull, Easton, Weston and Westport.
Bigelow Tea keeps its headquarters on Black Rock Turnpike in Fairfield, the same Connecticut town where Sacred Heart plays.
Penfield Reef Lighthouse stands in Long Island Sound off the coast of Fairfield Beach in Sacred Heart's hometown of Fairfield, Connecticut.
Sacred Heart and Fairfield University together enroll more than 17,000 students in the town of Fairfield.
Sacred Heart's suburban campus covers more than 300 acres in Fairfield, about 50 miles northeast of New York City.
Sacred Heart acquired the former General Electric corporate headquarters near its main campus in Fairfield in 2016.
Sacred Heart University was founded in 1963 by Walter W. Curtis, bishop of the Diocese of Bridgeport, on the grounds of the former Notre Dame Catholic High School.
Sacred Heart's teams wear red and white, and the school's mascot is Big Red the Pioneer.
Keith Bennett became Sacred Heart's career scoring leader in 1983 and was a National Association of Basketball Coaches Division II All-American in 1981, 1982 and 1983.
Sacred Heart's alumni include actors Kevin Nealon, a former Saturday Night Live cast member, and John Ratzenberger.
Former Major League Baseball player and manager Bobby Valentine was hired as Sacred Heart's athletic director in 2013.
Dave Bike coached Sacred Heart from 1978 to 2013, posting a 528-500 record and winning the 1986 Division II national title.
Sacred Heart coach Anthony Latina played at Brandeis from 1991 to 1995 and was an assistant at UMass Lowell and Central Connecticut before joining the Pioneers' staff in 2005.
Anthony Latina has been Sacred Heart's head coach since 2013, when he was promoted after eight seasons as a Pioneers assistant.
Sacred Heart's 20-13 finish in 2019-20 was the only 20-win season in Anthony Latina's first 13 years as head coach.
Sacred Heart went 14-19 overall and 9-11 in league play last season, its second in the conference.
Sacred Heart was the ninth seed in last season's conference tournament, beating Iona 91-80 at Boardwalk Hall before falling to top-seeded Merrimack in the quarterfinals.
Sacred Heart and Fairfield University, both located in the town of Fairfield, met in the first round of the 2025 MAAC tournament, a 71-58 Pioneers win.
Sacred Heart won 77-71 at crosstown Fairfield on Feb. 8, 2025, during the Pioneers' first season in the same league as the Stags.
A crowd of 2,236 watched Fairfield edge Sacred Heart 92-87 on Feb. 5, 2026, in a meeting of the town of Fairfield's two universities.
Sacred Heart, Fairfield and Quinnipiac of Hamden give the Metro Conference three Connecticut members.
Sacred Heart and Merrimack entered the league together for the 2024-25 season.
Sacred Heart's athletic rivalry with in-state Central Connecticut State is known as the Constitution State Rivalry.

home_lines.text: The William H. Pitt Center, Sacred Heart's home floor on Park Avenue in Fairfield, opened on Aug. 17, 1997, at a cost of $13.8 million.
Sacred Heart's Pitt Center, formally the William H. Pitt Health and Recreation Center, has three levels and four basketball courts.
Sacred Heart's Pitt Center hosted the finals of the 2008 Northeast Conference men's basketball tournament.
The Pitt Center in Fairfield, home of Sacred Heart basketball since 1997, also housed the Connecticut Skyhawks of the United States Basketball League in 1998 and 1999.
Sacred Heart's Pitt Center is shared by the Pioneers' basketball, volleyball, wrestling and fencing teams.

lines.text: Rider earned its first NCAA Tournament bid in 1984, when John Carpenter's team won the East Coast Conference tournament with a 73-71 overtime win over top seed Bucknell.
Rider's first NCAA Tournament game came on March 13, 1984, at the Palestra in Philadelphia, where the 12th-seeded Broncs lost to Richmond, 89-65.
Darrick Suber drove for the winning basket in the final four seconds as Rider beat Wagner 65-64 in the 1993 Northeast Conference final in Lawrenceville and earned an NCAA Tournament bid.
Rider's 1993 NCAA Tournament trip ended in Nashville, where the 16th-seeded Broncs lost to top seed Kentucky, 96-52, on March 19, 1993.
Rider won back-to-back Northeast Conference tournaments under Kevin Bannon, beating Monmouth 62-56 in the 1994 final before falling to second-seeded Connecticut in the NCAA first round.
Darrick Suber remains Rider's career scoring leader with 2,219 points, ahead of Jerry Johnson at 2,047 and Jason Thompson at 2,040.
Rider has retired two men's basketball numbers: No. 4 for guard Darrick Suber and No. 1 for Jason Thompson, whose jersey went up in 2009.
Jason Thompson holds Rider's career records with 1,171 rebounds and 235 blocked shots.
Clair Bee founded varsity athletics at Rider in 1929, and his 1930 Rider team was the first in the nation to score 1,000 points in a single season.
Naismith Hall of Famer Clair Bee, author of the Chip Hilton books, coached Rider basketball for three seasons before winning two national championships at Long Island University.
Rider reached the Elite Eight of the 1957 NCAA small-college tournament after wins over Drexel, 63-61, and St. Michael's, 69-68.
Rider has won four MAAC regular-season titles, in 2002, 2005, 2008 and 2018.
Rider's 2017-18 team went 15-3 in the MAAC, sharing the regular-season title with Canisius and earning the No. 1 seed in the league tournament.
Rider beat No. 18 Mississippi State 88-74 on the road on Nov. 13, 2009.
Rider set program single-game records with 32 assists and 76.4 percent shooting in a 104-62 win at Manhattan in February 2024.
John Carpenter holds the Rider men's basketball record for coaching wins with 292.
Rider's home floor in Lawrenceville was renamed Canastra Hammer Arena in June 2026 for alumni Wayne and Jill Canastra, Class of 1972, and Jill's brother, Alan R. Hammer, Class of 1968.
Rider's gym, known for decades as Alumni Gym, was the first building on the Lawrenceville campus and opened with the school's 1958 commencement.
Seton Hall was the opponent for the first Rider basketball game in the Lawrenceville gym, the 1958-59 season opener.
Lawrence Township, home of Rider, was founded in 1697 as Maidenhead and renamed in 1816 for Captain James Lawrence, a War of 1812 naval hero who commanded the frigate Chesapeake.
Colonel Edward Hand's delaying action in Lawrence slowed British troops before the Second Battle of Trenton in January 1777, and Lawrence Township still marches to Trenton each year in his honor.
Rider's campus on Route 206 in Lawrence Township sits about 3 miles north of Trenton and 5 miles south of Princeton.
Lawrence Township, home of Rider, is also home to The Lawrenceville School and the headquarters of Bristol-Myers Squibb and Educational Testing Service.
Rider was founded in Trenton in 1865 as Trenton Business College and moved to its Lawrence Township campus in 1959.
Rider teams were first called the Roughriders, a name chosen by Clair Bee, before a Rider News sportswriter, George Abbott, began calling them the Broncos in 1949.
Rider's costumed mascot is AJ the Bronc.
Rider's cranberry school color traces to the cranberry bogs of Andrew J. Rider, the school's first president.
Rider and Saint Peter's, two New Jersey schools, first played in 1942-43 and became MAAC rivals in 1998-99.
Rider, Monmouth and Saint Peter's, three schools about an hour apart, launched the hOURglass Rivalry in 2013.
Jason Thompson, picked 12th overall by Sacramento in the 2008 NBA Draft, played eight NBA seasons with the Kings, Warriors and Raptors after leaving Rider.
Digger Phelps, later the longtime coach at Notre Dame, was a Rider reserve and a graduate assistant on the 1963-64 Rider team that ended NYU's 23-year home winning streak.
Kevin Baggett, a two-time MAAC Coach of the Year in 2015 and 2018, joined Rider's staff in 2006-07 from UMBC and was named head coach on May 24, 2012.
Kevin Baggett is in his 15th season as Rider's head coach, having gone 210-227 overall and 142-130 in league play through 2025-26.
Rider finished 4-25 overall and 3-17 in the MAAC in 2025-26, closing with a 76-61 loss at Siena.
Rider is playing its first season in the Metro Conference, the new name the MAAC took on July 1, 2026.
Ryan Thompson, fourth on Rider's career scoring list with 1,879 points, returned to his alma mater this season as an assistant coach after five years on Rowan's staff.
Rider's 2026-27 schedule includes a 20-game Metro Conference slate, with the conference tournament set for March 4-9 at Jim Whelan Boardwalk Hall.

home_lines.text: Canastra Hammer Arena, Rider's home court in Lawrenceville, seats 1,650.
Rider's home court in Lawrenceville is known as the Broncs' Zoo.
Rider's gym in Lawrenceville hosted the Northeast Conference men's basketball championship game three straight years, from 1993 to 1995.

lines.text: Saint Peter's played its first men's basketball season in 1930-31, the same year the Jersey City school reopened after closing in 1918.
In 2022 Saint Peter's became the first No. 15 seed to reach the NCAA Elite Eight, beating Kentucky, Murray State and Purdue before falling to North Carolina.
Saint Peter's earned its first NCAA Tournament win in its fourth try, beating No. 2 seed Kentucky 85-79 in overtime at Gainbridge Fieldhouse in Indianapolis in 2022.
Saint Peter's reached the 2022 Elite Eight by beating No. 3 seed Purdue 67-64 in the Sweet 16 at the Wells Fargo Center in Philadelphia on March 25.
The 2021-22 Saint Peter's team finished No. 24 in the final USA Today Coaches poll, the program's first top-25 ranking, and was honored with a parade through Jersey City.
Saint Peter's has made five NCAA Tournament trips, in 1991, 1995, 2011, 2022 and 2024, and owns a 3-5 record in the event.
Saint Peter's 1967-68 team went 24-4 and averaged 94 points per game, and its 24 wins remain the program record for a season.
Saint Peter's is 2-0 all-time against Duke, winning 100-71 in the NIT on March 18, 1968, and 77-74 on December 27, 1971, both in New York.
Saint Peter's has played in the NIT 12 times, and its best run came in 1968, when the Peacocks reached the semifinals and finished fourth.
Saint Peter's won the 2024 MAAC title as a No. 5 seed, getting there on a buzzer-beater in a 62-60 semifinal win over top-seeded Quinnipiac in Atlantic City.
Saint Peter's beat Fairfield 68-63 in the 2024 MAAC championship game in Atlantic City as Corey Washington scored 24 points.
Saint Peter's won the 2017 CIT championship to cap a 23-win season under John Dunne.
Keydren Clark scored 3,058 points at Saint Peter's from 2002 to 2006 and led all of Division I in scoring in both 2004 and 2005.
Keydren Clark set the scoring record for the Saint Peter's home arena in Jersey City with 44 points in a 94-85 win over St. Francis (N.Y.) on November 27, 2002.
Saint Peter's forward KC Ndefo became the first player in program history with 300 career blocks and was the 2022 Lefty Driesell National Defensive Player of the Year.
Elnardo Webster played on the Saint Peter's team that reached the 1968 NIT semifinals and went on to play one season in the American Basketball Association.
Will Durant, who won the 1968 Pulitzer Prize for General Nonfiction, is a Saint Peter's alumnus.
Shaheen Holloway went 64-57 in four seasons at Saint Peter's, led the 2022 Elite Eight run and was hired by Seton Hall, his alma mater, on March 30, 2022.
John Dunne coached Saint Peter's for 12 seasons and won the 2011 MAAC title as a No. 4 seed, beating top-seeded Fairfield and second-seeded Iona.
The Saint Peter's home arena opened on November 29, 1975, at a cost of $6 million, and the Peacocks lost the first game there to Dartmouth, 68-67.
The Victor R. Yanitelli, S.J. Recreational Life Center, which houses the Saint Peter's basketball arena, is named for the school's 17th president.
Saint Peter's opened the renovated Run Baby Run Arena on November 1, 2021, with a 90-66 exhibition win over New Jersey City University.
The Saint Peter's Peacocks nickname echoes Pavonia, the original name of the Jersey City area, which means land of the peacock.
Saint Peter's made the peacock its official mascot in 1930, when the Jersey City school reopened after being closed from 1918 to 1930.
Saint Peter's was chartered by the New Jersey Legislature on April 3, 1872, and is one of 27 Jesuit colleges and universities in the United States and the only one in New Jersey.
Saint Peter's moved to its Kennedy Boulevard campus in 1936 and officially became Saint Peter's University on August 17, 2012.
The Saint Peter's mascot is Peter the Peacock.
Jersey City, home of Saint Peter's, counted 292,449 residents in the 2020 census, second in New Jersey only to Newark.
Jersey City, home of Saint Peter's, faces Manhattan across the Hudson River, and most of Ellis Island lies within the city's limits.
Journal Square, the Jersey City neighborhood just north of the Saint Peter's campus, takes its name from The Jersey Journal, which moved there in 1911.
Liberty State Park in Jersey City, home of Saint Peter's, opened on Flag Day 1976 and covers 1,212 acres.
Jersey City's Exchange Place district, home to Saint Peter's neighbors on the waterfront and known as Wall Street West, is one of the largest financial centers in the United States.
Saint Peter's and fellow New Jersey school Rider meet in the Hourglass rivalry, a series that dates to the 1942-43 season.
Bashir Mason, hired April 12, 2022, is the 16th head coach at Saint Peter's after a decade at Wagner, where he won three NEC regular-season titles.
Saint Peter's coach Bashir Mason was a four-year starter at Drexel and the first CAA Defensive Player of the Year in 2003-04.
Saint Peter's went 14-6 in league play last season to finish second among 13 teams, including a perfect 10-0 in conference games at home.
Saint Peter's season ended last March with a 74-55 loss to Fairfield in the league quarterfinals in Atlantic City, leaving the No. 2 seed Peacocks at 17-12.
Saint Peter's guard Bryce Eaton was a unanimous pick for the 2026-27 preseason All-Metro Conference first team.
Saint Peter's is playing its first season in the Metro Conference, the new name the MAAC took on July 1, 2026.
Saint Peter's opens Metro Conference play on December 2 at Manhattan in Riverdale, N.Y.
Saint Peter's and the other 12 Metro Conference teams are competing for 10 spots in the league tournament, set for March 4 to 9 in Atlantic City.

home_lines.text: Saint Peter's plays in Run Baby Run Arena, named by alumnus Thomas P. Mac Mahon for his 1967-68 teammates after his $5 million lead gift funded the renovation.
Run Baby Run Arena seats 3,200 for Saint Peter's men's basketball, with collapsible bleachers covering two of the main gym's three courts.
Run Baby Run Arena sits at 2641 Kennedy Boulevard in Jersey City on the site of the old Collins Memorial Gymnasium, and its building also houses an 8-lane pool.

lines.text: Siena first fielded a men's basketball team in 1938, the year after the school's founding in 1937.
Siena won its first NCAA Division I tournament game in 1989, when the 14th-seeded Saints beat third-seeded Stanford 80-78.
Ronald Moore's 3-pointer with 3.9 seconds left in the second overtime gave Siena a 74-72 win over Ohio State in the 2009 NCAA tournament in Dayton, Ohio.
In March 2026, 16th-seeded Siena led top-seeded Duke 43-32 at halftime, the first No. 16 seed to lead a No. 1 by double digits at the break, before losing 71-65.
Siena is 4-7 in the NCAA tournament across seven Division I appearances, the latest coming in 2026 after a 16-year absence.
Siena beat top-seeded Merrimack 64-54 in Atlantic City to win the 2026 MAAC tournament, the seventh conference tournament title in program history.
Siena won three straight MAAC championships from 2008 to 2010 and won 38 consecutive games at its downtown Albany arena in that stretch.
Siena's Doremus Bennerman scored an NIT-record 174 points in five games in 1994, including 51 against Kansas State in the third-place game at Madison Square Garden.
Siena has retired five men's basketball numbers: Marc Brown's 4, Billy Harrell's 10, Doremus Bennerman's 23, Kenny Hasbrouck's 41 and Fred Shear's 50.
Marc Brown is Siena's career scoring leader with 2,284 points.
Siena won the 2014 College Basketball Invitational, beating Fresno State two games to one in the best-of-three finals.
Siena, then known as the Indians, won the National Catholic Invitational Tournament in Albany in 1950.
Siena played Niagara in a six-overtime game in 1952-53, at the time the longest game in NCAA history.
Fred Shear, whose No. 50 is retired at Siena, averaged 20.3 points a game from 1969 to 1973 and reached 1,000 points in 52 games, the fewest in program history.
Siena gained Division I status in 1976, four years after Bill Kirsch became the school's head coach and athletic director.
Albany has been the official capital of New York State since 1797.
Albany traces its history more than 400 years to the 17th-century Dutch settlement of Fort Orange.
Albany's Washington Park, created in the 1870s, hosts the city's Tulip Festival every spring.
Albany's Empire State Plaza has three reflecting pools set between the towering buildings of New York state government.
Siena's campus is in Loudonville, a hamlet in the town of Colonie just north of Albany that is named for John Campbell, the 4th Earl of Loudoun.
Municipal and state governments employ around a quarter of the Albany region's workforce, with health care, technology, service and manufacturing also leading industries.
Siena was founded in 1937 by seven Franciscan friars sent by Fr. Thomas Plassmann, then president of St. Bonaventure College, to the former Garrett estate in Loudonville.
Siena opened as St. Bernardine of Siena College, named for a 15th-century Franciscan preacher, and took the name Siena College in 1968.
Siena College became Siena University after New York's Board of Regents approved the change in July 2025.
Siena played the 1988-89 season without a nickname and adopted the name Saints on March 16, 1989.
Siena and its Franciscan sister school St. Bonaventure have played for the Br. Ed Coughlin Franciscan Cup since 2010.
Siena's annual Gold Rush game against archrival Iona encourages fans to wear gold.
Siena has played Iona more times than any other opponent, and the two programs rank first and second in MAAC history in league wins, regular-season titles and tournament titles.
Siena entered its 98th meeting with I-87 rival Marist in February 2026 holding a 64-33 lead in the series.
Former Siena guard Jalen Pickett, the 2020 MAAC Player of the Year, was taken 32nd overall in the 2023 NBA draft after finishing his college career at Penn State.
Siena's Billy Harrell, whose No. 10 is retired, was drafted by both the NBA's Minneapolis Lakers and baseball's Cleveland Indians.
Paul Hewitt went 66-27 in three seasons at Siena before leading Georgia Tech to the 2004 national championship game.
Fran McCaffery went 112-51 at Siena from 2005 to 2010, winning three MAAC tournament titles before leaving for Iowa.
Gerry McNamara went 37-30 in two seasons at Siena and took the Saints to the 2026 NCAA tournament before leaving for Syracuse.
Nevada Smith, a former Marquette assistant on Shaka Smart's staff, was named Siena's 20th head coach on April 1, 2026.
Siena coach Nevada Smith went 135-116 in five NBA G League seasons with Rio Grande Valley and Sioux Falls, and 14 of his players were promoted to the NBA.
Siena coach Nevada Smith set the Bethany College record with 313 made 3-pointers as a four-year starter from 1998 to 2002.
Siena went 23-12 last season, finished third in the MAAC and won the conference tournament.
Siena is playing its 86th season of men's basketball.
This is Siena's 38th season of league play and its first since the MAAC was renamed the Metro Conference on July 1, 2026.
The Metro Conference tournament, where Siena defends its title, runs March 4-10 at Jim Whelan Boardwalk Hall in Atlantic City, N.J.

home_lines.text: MVP Arena, Siena's home at 51 South Pearl Street in downtown Albany, opened on Jan. 30, 1990, with a Frank Sinatra concert.
The downtown Albany building Siena calls home was Knickerbocker Arena, Pepsi Arena and the Times Union Center before becoming MVP Arena on Jan. 1, 2022.
Siena's largest regular-season crowd at its downtown Albany arena is 14,743, set against Syracuse on Nov. 27, 2004.
Siena's first game at the downtown Albany arena was a 71-53 MAAC tournament win over Canisius on March 3, 1990, before 12,231 fans.
Through the 2023-24 season, nearly 2.8 million fans had attended 434 Siena games at the downtown Albany arena, an average of 6,411.
